country.comment: Empirical study conducted in two rural villages (Madiba and Enqabeni) in Winnie Madikizela-Mandela Local Municipality, Alfred Nzo District Municipality, Eastern Cape Province, South Africa.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Abstract; PDF p. 3, Methodology — Study area; PDF p. 6, Table 1

effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive mixed-methods results with chi-square goodness-of-fit tests; no regression or causal point estimate linking institutional variables to water outcomes is reported.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive mixed-methods findings (no causal numeric effect estimate): Despite Section 27(1)(b) of the Constitution and post-1994 water legislation, 100% (n = 205) of surveyed households in Enqabeni and 70% (n = 92) in Madiba relied on untreated open water bodies, while 30% (n = 39) in Madiba used an unpumped open community borehole (X2 = 21; df = 1; p < 0.0001) after its pump broke in 2012 and four community taps (installed in 2008) failed by 2016 without municipal repair. 100% of households in both Enqabeni (n = 205) and Madiba (n = 131) reported their water was unsafe/untreated, 68% (n = 139) in Enqabeni and 52% (n = 68) in Madiba traveled >5 km daily to fetch water, and only 17% in Enqabeni (n = 35) and 17% in Madiba (n = 22) could afford vendor water for drinking and cooking; Madiba received Tuesday municipal water-truck deliveries capped at 25 L/person whereas Enqabeni received none. Key barriers identified were legacy homeland infrastructure deficits, municipal underfunding (Alfred Nzo District Municipality received R21,000,000 of R48,471,849 requested in 2021/2022), ignored community repair complaints to the municipality and ward councilor, and corruption/mismanagement (reported by 100% of respondents in both villages, including a traditional leader selling free municipal COVID-19 rainwater-harvesting tanks in Enqabeni).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 5–10, Results (Water sources, transportation, and consumption; Infrastructural challenges; Institutional challenges; Corruption and mismanagement of funds)

mechanism_certainty.comment: Mixed-methods primary study (design ceiling = 2) that directly documents institutional and administrative mechanisms through key-informant interviews with municipal officials, ward councilors, and traditional leaders, household surveys, and field observations (specifically municipal budget shortfalls, unheeded repair complaints to municipal authorities and ward councilors, unmaintained communal infrastructure, and local elite capture/sale of free municipal rainwater tanks).
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 6–10, Results — Barriers to accessing drinking water (Infrastructural challenges, Institutional challenges, Corruption and mismanagement of funds)

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines rural former-homeland (Ciskei) spatial exclusion and erratic settlement patterns hindering bulk/reticulation extension (ELIGIBILITY: service_area, planning), municipal budget planning/intergovernmental underfunding and coordination gaps (political_coordination), corruption/elite diversion of free rainwater tanks and municipal funds (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: discretion) alongside lack of participatory decision-making (participation), and non-implementation of constitutional/statutory water rights with unanswered community repair complaints to the municipality and ward councilor (ENFORCEMENT: complaint).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, service_area, planning, discretion, complaint, participation, political_coordination
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 2–3, Conceptual framework; PDF pp. 6–11, Results & Discussion

outcome_flags.comment: Measures primary household drinking water sources and >5 km fetching distances (water_access), absence/breakdown of piped taps and boreholes (service_coverage, service_continuity), untreated livestock-contaminated water (service_quality), daily household volume used and 25 L/person municipal truck cap vs statutory minimum (service_quantity), and inability of grant-reliant households to purchase clean vendor water or diverted tanks (affordability).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary mixed-methods study combining a quantitative systematic random household questionnaire survey (n = 336, analyzed in SPSS with descriptive frequencies and chi-square tests) and qualitative semi-structured key-informant interviews plus field observations (analyzed via thematic content analysis).

sample_size.comment: 10% systematic random sample of households in both villages (205 of 2,048 households in Enqabeni; 131 of 1,307 households in Madiba; total n = 336 households, excluding 20 pretest respondents who were not part of the study). Exact count of purposively sampled key informants (municipal officials, ward councilors, traditional leaders) is not stated in the paper.
sample_size.value: 336 households across 2 rural villages (205 households in Enqabeni and 131 households in Madiba) for interviewer-administered questionnaires; plus semi-structured interviews with purposively sampled municipal officials, ward councilors, and traditional leaders (exact N not reported)

study_design.value: Mixed-methods cross-sectional study combining systematic random household questionnaire survey (descriptive statistics and chi-square tests), semi-structured key-informant interviews (thematic content analysis), and field observations

evidence_quotes.quote: The study was conducted in Madiba and Enqabeni rural villages that fall under Winnie Madikizela-Mandela Local Municipality, which is situated in the Alfred Nzo District Municipality in the Eastern Cape Province (Figure 1).

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 5, Results — Water sources, transportation, and consumption
evidence_quotes.quote: When asked about their main source of water, all the respondents (100%; n = 205) in Enqabeni village indicated that they obtained water from open water bodies (rivers, wetlands, streams, springs and ponds).

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 5, Results — Water sources, transportation, and consumption
evidence_quotes.quote: In Madiba village, 70% (n = 92) of the respondents indicated that they obtained water from open water bodies, and the remaining 30% (n = 39) relied on one community borehole (X2 = 21; df = 1; p < 0.0001).

Similarly, the four community taps that were supplying water to the local communities also broke and were never repaired by the municipality. As a result, since 2016, the communities in Madiba village have not have access to tap water.
This means that the Constitution and policies related to providing water services have not yet been implemented, at least in Enqabeni or Madiba villages.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 9, Results — Corruption and mismanagement of funds
evidence_quotes.quote: The study found that at some point, the traditional leader was selling the tanks that were meant to be given to communities free of charge.
